Enhancing Early Plant Growth in Regolith: Evaluation of Germination Methods, Growth 
Media, Pre-Planting Treatments, and Alternative Watering Techniques 
Team Name: Academic Magnet 
Team ID: 20638 
Neva Aygar, Leah Bagg, Alexandra Eastman, Caitlin Farr, Chloe Hwang, Helina Lloyd, Hannah 
McLaughlin, Zavier Nutting, Yamil Perez, Yidong Ye, Yiqing Ye, Luke Zheltov 
Challenge Category: High School

3 
 
 
Abstract 
As long-duration lunar missions and extraterrestrial habitation become increasingly 
feasible, developing sustainable agricultural systems in resource-limited environments is critical. 
Our research, conducted as part of NASA’s Plant the Moon Challenge, evaluated how different 
germination stages, planting methods, and soil amendments influence early plant growth in 
simulated regolith—a substrate characterized by low nutrient content, poor water retention, and 
limited permeability. We hypothesized that incorporating nutrient-rich Miracle-Gro Garden Soil 
and moisture-retentive gelatin into regolith-based mixtures and transplanting seeds after radicle 
or root hair emergence would enhance early plant growth in regolith-dominant substrates. Six 
bean varieties were tested across six medium types, ranging from 100% regolith to formulated 
blends containing Miracle-Gro and gelatin. Control variables—including light, soil moisture, and 
temperature—were monitored using a BBC micro:bit consistent conditions without manual data 
collection. As expected, direct planting into high-regolith media led to poor germination and limited 
growth. However, transplanting seeds after paper towel pre-germination consistently improved 
survival and early development across all media. The 20G composite mix (50% regolith, 30% 
garden soil, 20% gelatin) yielded the most consistent success, balancing nutrient enrichment and 
water retention. In addition, Broad Windsor Fava beans exhibited strong adaptability, even in pure 
regolith. To further promote growth, a passive self-watering system was implemented to provide 
steady subsurface moisture and improve root development. Our findings highlight a multi-faceted 
approach—targeting pre-plant stage, media optimization, and water delivery—to support early 
plant development in regolith simulants. These insights not only inform space agriculture design 
but also present potential applications for sustainable farming in arid, nutrient-poor terrestrial 
environments. Future research should focus on optimizing gelatin concentrations, assessing plant 
responses under lunar gravity, and evaluating long-term growth outcomes to strengthen 
extraterrestrial agricultural viability.

1. Introduction 
As humanity prepares for extended space missions and potential lunar habitation, the 
development of sustainable food production methods in extraterrestrial environments has become 
a research priority. NASA’s Artemis Project, which lays the groundwork for future Mars missions, 
highlights the urgent need for creating closed-loop life support systems (Scheinkman et al., 2024). 
Plants play a pivotal role in these systems—not only as a food source but also by recycling carbon 
dioxide into oxygen, thereby contributing to atmospheric regulation (Shymanovich & Kiss, 2022). 
The Plant the Moon Challenge supports this initiative by involving students and emerging 
researchers in experimental research focused on plant cultivation under simulated lunar 
conditions. The regolith simulants used in the challenge are designed to replicate the physical 
and chemical characteristics of lunar soil, which is inherently nutrient-deficient and exhibits poor 
water retention and aeration. The objective of the challenge is to develop resource-efficient 
strategies that optimize plant growth in these restrictive conditions—an essential consideration 
for achieving long-term sustainability in off-Earth environments. 
To address this, our study explores resource-efficient approaches for promoting early 
seedling development using readily available or replicable materials. We investigated how 
variations in seed developmental stages and growth media composition affect plant establishment 
in regolith simulants. By focusing on reducing terrestrial soil usage, our media primarily relied on 
regolith simulant supplemented with nutrient-rich additives such as Miracle-Gro Garden Mix and 
gelatin. These amendments were selected to counteract the simulant’s deficiencies in essential 
nutrients—particularly nitrogen—and improve its poor water retention and permeability. 
Regolith poses several barriers to plant cultivation. It is predominantly composed of silicon 
dioxide (SiO₂), aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃), calcium oxide (CaO), and iron oxide (FeO), with SiO₂ 
alone comprising approximately 50% of its makeup. According to research by Van Nhan Le, 
elevated SiO₂ concentrations significantly inhibit plant growth, resulting in reductions in both 
biomass and plant height. Furthermore, regolith lacks essential macronutrients such as nitrogen

2 
 
 
(N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K), and its poor water retention and low permeability 
severely limit root development (Ming & Henninger, 1994). This led us to conclude that there is a 
necessity for incorporating nutrient-dense and moisture-retentive amendments to support plant 
viability. 
To overcome the inherent limitations of nutrient-deficient regolith simulant, we 
incorporated Miracle-Gro Garden Soil, a nutrient-rich substrate formulated to promote healthy 
plant development. This garden soil comprises sphagnum peat moss, perlite, compost, yucca, 
processed forest products, coir, and a slow-release fertilizer blend containing polymer-coated 
ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate, potassium sulfate, and calcium phosphate (marsh, 
2025). Together, these components were able to enhance nutrient availability, improve water 
retention, and support root structure, addressing two of the most significant challenges posed by 
regolith: poor fertility and limited water-holding capacity. 
Specifically, each component plays a distinct role. Sphagnum peat moss plays a vital role 
in both moisture and nutrient retention (Bengtsson et al., 2020). It sequesters carbon dioxide and 
nutrients, reducing leaching while maintaining soil fertility. Its fibrous structure allows it to absorb 
large quantities of water while preserving soil aeration, helping to keep the root zone both moist 
and oxygenated. Perlite further enhances soil aeration and improves nutrient uptake (Ebadollahi 
et al., 2019). Its porous nature allows for better oxygen flow around plant roots and supports 
nitrogen absorption and overall root function, indirectly boosting plant growth. Compost, made of 
organic matter, enriches the soil by adding nutrients and improving microbial activity. It enhances 
overall soil structure and fertility, creating a healthier environment for plant development. Yucca, 
a drought-tolerant starchy root plant, contributes resilience to the soil mix (Benito et al., 2023). Its 
natural stress resistance is beneficial in dry or extreme conditions, making it an important 
component when simulating the harsh, arid environment of regolith. Coir, derived from coconut 
fiber, supports water retention, drainage, and air porosity. Its use has been shown to increase the 
availability of secondary nutrients such as calcium, magnesium, sulfur, chlorine, and zinc, as

3 
 
 
reviewed by Vatansever et al. (Vatansever et al., 2017), contributing to healthier, more balanced 
plant development. Finally, the fertilizer blend delivers essential macronutrients. Ammonium 
nitrate and ammonium phosphate supply nitrogen (N), which is critical for chlorophyll production 
and protein synthesis (Song et al., 2025). Ammonium phosphate and calcium phosphate provide 
phosphorus (P), vital for ATP production, DNA synthesis, and root development (Yin et al., 2019). 
Potassium sulfate delivers potassium (K), which enhances photosynthetic activity, enzymatic 
processes, and stomatal regulation (Yin et al., 2019). Studies, including those by Preeti Rani and 
others, indicate that potassium and calcium phosphate treatments can significantly improve 
biomass and enzymatic regulation under drought stress. 
In addition to Miracle-Gro Garden Soil, gelatin was used for its potential benefits in water 
management and nitrogen fixation. Wilson et al. (Wilson et al., 2018) found a positive correlation 
between gelatin capsule content and plant growth, likely due to gelatin's amino acid profile 
enhancing nitrogen availability. Ming and Henninger (Ming & Henninger, 1994) also emphasized 
the need to improve “air and fluid movement parameters” in regolith-based systems. In our study, 
gelatin was first dissolved in water and allowed to solidify, then incorporated into the media at 
specified volume ratios—particularly in regolith-rich mixtures—to mitigate compaction and 
enhance fluid dynamics. 
We hypothesized that transplanting seeds at a more advanced developmental stage—
specifically at radicle emergence or root hair formation—using the paper towel germination 
method would significantly improve seedling establishment and early growth, particularly in media 
with high regolith content. Incorporating Miracle-Gro Garden Soil and gelatin into regolith-based 
media, while maintaining a majority regolith composition to reflect realistic lunar resource 
constraints, would enhance plant growth. Specifically, we anticipated that Miracle-Gro would 
improve nutrient availability and soil structure, while gelatin, due to its water-retentive and amino 
acid-rich properties, would further increase moisture retention and support faster seedling 
development under simulated lunar conditions.

4 
 
 
Beans were chosen for this study because of their exceptionally high nutrient content, 
including essential minerals such as iron and zinc, protein, and various phytochemical compounds 
(Mullins & Arjmandi, 2021). While beans are not the only plant-based protein source, they are 
unique in providing the essential amino acid lysine, which is often deficient in plant-based diets 
that do not include beans. In addition to their protein content, beans are also rich in dietary fiber 
and have a lower score on the glycemic index (Messina, 2014). Furthermore, beans have a 
relatively short life cycle, with harvest maturity reached within 65 days (Clavijo Michelangeli et al., 
2013), making them an ideal candidate for space agriculture experiments where time and 
resource efficiency are critical. 
2. Materials/Methods 
2.1 Materials 
This study utilized various materials, including growth media such as Lunar Highlands 
Simulant Engineering Grade (LHS-1E), all-purpose garden soil (Miracle-Gro, Home Depot), and 
original unflavored gelatin (Knox, Harris Teeter). The seeds used in the experiment included 
Broad Windsor Fava Beans (Isla’s Garden Seed Company, Amazon), Tendergreen Improved 
organic Beans (Ferry-Morse, Home Depot), Kentucky Wonder organic Beans (Ferry-Morse, 
Home Depot), Green Mung Beans (Asian Taste, H & L Asian Market), Burpee’s Stringless Green 
Pod Beans (Burpee, Home Depot), and Great Northern Beans (Harris Teeter). Measurement tools 
included Microbit sensors; a 4-in-1 soil moisture meter (Yamron, Amazon) for assessing plant 
temperature, soil moisture, pH, and light intensity; a Compass Series Portable Balance (1200 g × 
0.1 g, CX1201, Ohaus); a 100 mL graduated cylinder; and a ruler. 
Growth Medium

5 
 
 
Seeds 
 
2.2 Greenhouse design 
The growth setup consisted of a large cardboard box (18 x 18 x 24 inches) lined with 
aluminum foil to optimize light reflection and equipped with a T9 9-Inch Circline Fluorescent Lamp 
(3000K warm white) (Lights of America FCL30EX-L 27K, Amazon). The lamp was programmed 
to operate on a 16-hour light and 8-hour dark cycle using a 24-hour indoor plug-in basic 
mechanical timer (Home Depot), mimicking greenhouse conditions. 
 
2.3 Microbit sensors 
To collect environmental data, we employed the BBC micro:bit, a compact microcontroller 
with an array of integrated sensors, including a light sensor and temperature sensor. We also 
utilized a kit that came with additional sensors, including a dirt moisture sensor and humidity 
sensor. The micro:bit was programmed using the Microsoft MakeCode editor, which allowed for 
the development of custom scripts to automate data logging at defined intervals.

6 
 
 
The device was configured to record light levels, temperature, and soil moisture at 60 
second intervals over the course of the experimental period. Data was stored locally on the 
micro:bit and later extracted via USB connection for further analysis. All sensor data were 
timestamped to ensure accurate temporal alignment during analysis. 
 
The micro:bit was selected due to its ease of use, portability, and suitability for real-time 
data acquisition. Calibration of the onboard sensors was conducted prior to deployment to ensure 
accuracy. The device was secured in a stable position throughout the data collection process to 
minimize extraneous variables.

2.4 The Water and Paper Towel Germination Method 
The water germination method involves submerging seeds in water to soften the seed 
coat and accelerate germination, particularly for seeds with hard shells or those requiring rapid 
hydration. In this experiment, seeds were fully submerged in room-temperature water within 10 
cm Petri dishes and kept in a warm, dark environment. Germination progress was observed every 
24 hours. 
The paper towel method provides optimal moisture and air circulation while preventing 
waterlogging. Seeds were wrapped in a damp—but not overly wet—paper towel and placed in 10 
cm Petri dishes. The dishes were positioned vertically inside a container with a small amount of 
water, allowing the paper towel to absorb moisture without submerging the seeds. The setup was 
then kept in a warm, dark environment to promote germination. Seeds were monitored daily.

8 
 
 
 
2.5 Gelatin Preparation 
Gelatin was prepared by bringing three cups of water to a boil, sprinkling one ounce of 
gelatin over one cup of water, and allowing it to stand for one minute. The hot water was then 
added while stirring continuously for five minutes. The mixture was subsequently refrigerated until 
firm. 
2.6 Growth Medium Preparation 
Six distinct growth media compositions were prepared for this study: 100% garden soil 
(control, 100S); 100% regolith (100R); a 50:50 (v/v) mixture of regolith and garden soil (50SR); a 
50:50 (v/v) mixture of garden soil and gelatin (50SG); a 50:50 (v/v) mixture of regolith and gelatin 
(50G); and a composition consisting of 50% regolith, 30% garden soil, and 20% gelatin (20G). 
2.7 Planting Procedure 
Appropriately sized garden pots with drainage holes were selected, cleaned, and dried. A 
sheet of tissue paper was placed at the bottom of each pot to prevent leakage of the growth 
medium. Each pot was then filled with its respective growth medium, pressed lightly to 
approximately 60% capacity. Using chopsticks, evenly spaced holes, approximately half an inch 
deep, were created in each pot. Seeds were planted according to species, with one to four seeds 
per hole. The holes were then covered with the respective growth medium, and the surface was 
leveled. The pots were watered slowly using the graduated cylinder to ensure the seeds were 
fully covered while avoiding over-saturation. They were then transferred to a greenhouse, where 
a timer-controlled lighting system maintained a photoperiod of 16 hours of light and 8 hours of 
darkness.

9 
 
 
2.8 Self-watering system 
 
The self-watering system was constructed by drilling holes into the lids of Tupperware 
containers and threading half-inch-wide cloth strips through both these openings and the drainage 
holes of standard garden pots, effectively linking the pots to the water reservoirs below. The soil 
media was added to the pots with the cloth strips positioned to remain exposed at the soil surface, 
ensuring upward capillary movement of water. Water was then added to the Tupperware 
containers to complete the self-watering system. Throughout the experiment, water levels were 
regularly monitored to maintain consistent contact between the cloth strips and the water, 
ensuring uninterrupted moisture delivery. 
 
2.9 Variables, Growth Monitoring, and Data Collection 
Plant growth monitoring took place over a designated period, during which various 
variables were recorded. These included emergence, plant height, leaf development, leaf size, 
number of leaves, and overall plant health. Additionally, soil properties such as pH level, moisture 
retention, temperature, and light intensity were measured for each growth medium. Watering was 
carefully regulated to maintain consistent soil moisture at approximately 60% across all test 
groups. 
3. Results 
3.1 Comparison of Germination Methods: Paper Towel vs. Water Soaking 
The paper towel method demonstrated consistently high germination success across all 
tested bean varieties (Figure 1A). Within 48 hours, germination was observed in Green Mung 
Beans (7/8, 88%), Kentucky Wonder Beans (5/6, 83%), Great Northern Beans (3/6, 50%), and

10 
 
 
Tendergreen Improved Beans (3/6, 50%). By 72 hours, complete germination (100%) was 
achieved in Green Mung Beans (8/8), Kentucky Wonder Beans (6/6), Tendergreen Improved 
Beans (6/6), and Broad Windsor Fava Beans (2/2). Additional germination was recorded in 
Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Beans (5/6, 83%) and Great Northern Beans (4/6, 67%). At this 
stage, radicle emergence was visibly noted in all germinated seeds. 
 
Figure 1. Germination rates and early seedling development of bean seeds using two germination 
methods. (A) Paper towel method: Germination progression of Green Mung Beans (n = 8), 
Kentucky Wonder Beans (n = 6), Tendergreen Improved (n = 6), Great Northern Beans (n = 6), 
Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Beans (n = 6), and Broad Windsor Fava Beans (n = 2). (B) Water 
germination method: Germination progression of the same bean varieties and sample sizes. 
Germination was assessed at 48, 72, and 96 hours. (C) and (D) Seedling growth observed on 
Day 7 following 108 hours of germination using the paper towel method (C) and water soaking 
method (D).

11 
 
 
By 96 hours, full germination (100%) was attained in Green Mung Beans, Kentucky 
Wonder Beans, Tendergreen Improved Beans, and Broad Windsor Fava Beans. Great Northern 
Beans also reached full germination (6/6) while Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Bean remained 
at 83% (5/6) (Figure 1B). By 108 hours, root hairs were visible in all successfully germinated 
seeds except Broad Windsor Fava Bean, which exhibited radicle emergence without further root 
hair development. 
In contrast, the water soaking method yielded significantly lower and more variable 
germination rates (Figure 1B). At 48 hours, only Green Mung Beans showed appreciable 
germination (3/8, 38%). By 72 hours, germination was observed in Broad Windsor Fava Beans 
(2/2, 100%) and Green Mung Beans (4/8, 50%), while the other varieties remained mostly 
ungerminated. At 96 hours, limited progress was observed in the remaining varieties: Green Mung 
Beans (6/8, 75%), Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Beans (4/6, 67%), Tendergreen Improved (1/6, 
17%), Kentucky Wonder (1/6, 17%), and Great Northern Beans (1/6, 17%). By 108 hours, only 
radicle emergence was observed and seedling development remained less advanced than that 
seen with the paper towel method, with no visible formation of root hairs. The reduced 
effectiveness of the water soaking method is likely due to hypoxic conditions caused by full 
submersion. Oxygen deprivation can inhibit aerobic metabolism, delay enzymatic activation, and 
disrupt key biochemical processes required for successful germination. 
After 108 hours, seeds from both methods were planted into plastic containers with 36 
egg-shaped holes, each with drilled holes at the bottom, filled with garden soil. Significant growth 
differences were observable after 7 days (Figure 1C-D). Overall, the paper towel method proved 
significantly more effective than the water-based germination approach. All tested seeds 
germinated within 72 hours using the paper towel technique, while the water method resulted in 
delayed, inconsistent, and incomplete germination.

12 
 
 
3.2 Variable Measurements 
 
Using the BBC micro:bit and 4-in-1 Soil Moisture Meter, we measured variables such as 
light, soil moisture, temperature and pH values. The BBC micro:bit recorded results comparable 
to the 4-in1 Soil Moisture Meter with temperatures ranging from 21°C to 24°C degrees celsius, 
which is within the optimal range of 20°C to 25°C according to De Ron et al. Soil moisture was 
kept consistently between 60% and 80%, light level was consistently around 200 with the values 
for the light sensor ranging from 0 (dark) to 255 (very bright) using the micro:bit, and pH values 
were taken using the 4-in-1 Soil Moisture Meter (Figure 2). The micro:bit was the preferred 
measurement device due to its passive data collection without the need for manual 
measurements. 
 
Figure 2. Daily pH measurements of six growth media over an 8-day period. Media included 100% 
soil (100S), 100% regolith (100R), 50% soil–50% regolith (50SR), 50% regolith–30% soil–20% 
gelatin (20G), 50% soil–50% gelatin (50SG), and 50% regolith–50% gelatin (50G). Values are 
presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD).

13 
 
 
3.3 Comparative Growth Performance Across Growth Media and Germination Stages 
Six distinct growth media were formulated to evaluate their effects on seed germination 
and early seedling development: 100% soil (100S) as a control, 100% regolith (100R), 50% soil–
50% regolith (50SR), 50% soil–50% gelatin (50SG), 50% regolith–30% soil–20% gelatin (20G), 
and 50% regolith–50% gelatin (50G).Five seed varieties—Kentucky Wonder, Green Mung, 
Tendergreen Improved, Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod, and Broad Windsor Fava—were planted 
on Day 1, following a 24-hour germination period using the water soaking method. Paper towel 
germination treatments began on Day 3, with Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Beans planted on 
Day 5 after radicle emergence, and Great Northern Beans planted on Day 8 following root hair 
appearance. To conserve regolith-based material, seeds at different developmental stages were 
planted into shared containers containing a single growth medium (Figure 3). 
 
Figure 3. Experimental setup in each pot with distinct growth media. 
 
Seedling emergence and early growth varied significantly across plant species, media 
types, and developmental stages at the time of planting. Both soil media composition and seed 
physiological readiness were critical determinants of germination success and early development. 
For instance, no seedlings developed in either 50G or 50SG, regardless of the germination stage. 
This failure was likely due to a combination of unfavorable physical and chemical conditions. The 
high gelatin content in both media caused excessive water retention and poor aeration, likely 
creating hypoxic conditions that inhibited root penetration and expansion. Additionally, the slightly

14 
 
 
acidic pH levels—5.61 ± 0.46 in 50SG and 5.95 ± 1.20 in 50G (Figure 2)—may have limited 
seedling viability by falling below the optimal pH range of pH 6-7 for most bean species (Marissa 
Schuh, 2024). Due to these limitations, only the results from the four remaining media types are 
presented in the following discussion. 
3.3.1 Comparative Growth Performance Across Growth Media 
Germination and sprouting of Green Mung Bean seeds, following a 24-hour water soak, 
was observed exclusively in the 100S medium, with emergence occurring on Day 6 (Table 1). 
(Table 1). No sprouting occurred in any regolith-containing media, suggesting that Green Mung 
Bean may be more sensitive to non-soil conditions during early development. Kentucky Wonder 
Beans failed to germinate in all tested media. Notably, this variety demonstrated the highest water 
absorption ratios among all tested seeds (Figure 4), which may have resulted in overhydration 
and subsequent seed rot prior to radicle emergence.

better growth in 100S than in 20G. Growth rates, defined by the slope of seedling height increase 
from emergence to Day 27, were comparable between 100S and 20G for Tendergreen. However, 
seedlings in 20G had reduced height and primary leaf area (Figure 5). In Burpee’s, both growth 
rate and leaf area were significantly lower in 20G than in 100S (Figure 6). By Day 18, Tendergreen 
reached a height of 13 inches with a primary leaf area of 7.4 in² in 100S, while Burpee’s reached 
12 inches with a primary leaf area of 5.9 in². In contrast, seedlings in 20G showed reduced growth. 
Tendergreen reached 8 inches and Burpee’s 6.5 inches, with smaller primary leaf areas of 3.9 in² 
in both. Developmental progression was also impacted as Tendergreen exhibited delayed leaf 
emergence in 20G, while Burpee’s displayed a slight acceleration, with primary and secondary 
leaves emerging on Days 12 and 16, respectively, compared to Days 13 and 17 in 100S (Table 
1).

17 
 
 
 
Figure 6. (A) Seedling height and (B) primary leaf area of Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Beans 
grown in 100S and 20G over time following a 24-hour water soaking treatment. 
 
Broad Windsor Fava Beans emerged successfully in all media types. Emergence 
occurred by Day 8 in 100S and 50SR, Day 12 in 20G, and Day 18 in 100R. By Day 18, seedling 
heights and primary leaf areas varied markedly: In 50SR, plants reached 11.5 inches in height 
with a primary leaf area of 1.2 in²; in 20G, they reached 9 inches with a primary leaf area of 1.7 
in²; in 100S, they reached 7.5 inches with a primary leaf area of 0.9 in²; and in 100R, they reached 
only 1 inch. Nevertheless, secondary leaf emergence in 100R occurred by Day 22—only three 
days after primary leaf formation—demonstrating developmental timing comparable to that in 
other media and underscoring the species’ adaptability under regolith stress (Table 1). 
Growth rates through Day 27 followed the order: 100R > 50SR > 20G > 100S. Despite 
delayed emergence, seedlings in 100R experienced a marked growth acceleration between Days 
18 and 27, ultimately exceeding the growth rates of seedlings that had emerged earlier (Figure 
7A). This suggests that an initial acclimation phase was necessary in regolith-based media before 
the initiation of compensatory growth. In contrast, while 100S supported early emergence, 
subsequent growth proceeded more gradually. 
Primary leaf area exhibited a distinct trend: 20G > 50SR > 100S > 100R (Figure 7B), which 
was mirrored by the number of leaves observed (Figure 7C). The limited leaf expansion and

18 
 
 
development in 100R align with the known limitations of pure regolith, including poor water 
retention and low nutrient availability. Although 100S was expected to support the greatest leaf 
development due to its high nutrient content and consistent moisture retention, primary leaf areas 
in this medium were smaller than those observed in both 20G and 50SR. This counterintuitive 
result suggests that the moderate incorporation of regolith may have improved certain soil 
properties, such as altered pH (Figure 2) or modified microbial interactions, that supported 
broader leaf expansion in Broad Windsor Fava Bean, despite the overall lower nutrient availability 
in regolith-containing media.

physical media properties on early plant establishment in lunar analog environments. Although 
slower to promote growth, 20G consistently supported successful development in multiple species 
(Tables 1-2 and Figures 5-8), suggesting its potential as a balanced medium that moderates the 
trade-off between nutrient content and soil structure. In a parallel experiment, we investigated 
whether pre-germinating seeds to defined developmental stages could enhance establishment 
and early growth in regolith-based media.

3.3.2 Comparative Growth Performance Across Germination Stages 
As mentioned earlier, on Day 5, Burpee’s Stringless Garden Pod Bean seeds that had 
reached the radicle emergence stage via the paper towel germination method were transplanted 
into all six media types—100S, 100R, 50SR, 20G, 50SG, and 50G—adjacent to seeds from the 
initial 24-hour water soaking group in order to conserve regolith resources. Emergence from

21 
 
 
seeds at the radicle emergence stage occurred rapidly within 3–4 days across four media, 100S, 
100R, 50SR, and 20G, in contrast to the 24 hour water soaking method, which resulted in 
emergence only in 100S and 20G. By Day 14 (equivalent to Day 18 from the original planting 
timeline), seedlings in 50SR reached the greatest height (13.5 inches) with a primary leaf area of 
6.5 in², followed by 100S (12.5 inches, 10.2 in²), 20G (11 inches, 8.2 in²), and 100R (7.5 inches, 
5.9 in²). Compared to the 24 hour soaking group, development was markedly accelerated. 
Secondary leaves emerged as early as Day 10 in 100S, Day 11 in both 50SR and 20G, and Day 
12 in 100R (Table 1). Daily measurements of seedling height and leaf area (Figures 9 vs. 6), 
along with the number of leaves by Day 27 (Figure 10), confirmed enhanced growth and 
accelerated development. Specifically, seedlings in 20G and 50SR exhibited growth comparable 
to those in 100S. These findings suggest that pre-germination to the radicle stage significantly 
improves early seedling establishment, even under suboptimal conditions such as pure regolith.

For Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Beans, the combination of paper towel pre-
germination to the radicle stage with either 20G or 50SR media supported seedling development 
comparable to that observed in 100S. In Great Northern Beans, 20G combined with paper towel

root hair development displayed unexpectedly strong stem growth. This may reflect adaptive root 
behavior in response to surface moisture or aeration gradients within the regolith. These 
observations informed the implementation of a self-watering system to support seedling growth 
in 100R following transplanting at the root hair stage. By maintaining consistent moisture levels 
and eliminating the need for manual watering, this approach offers a practical solution for 
promoting seedling establishment in pure regolith—a medium that otherwise challenges plant 
growth due to its low water retention and poor structural properties. In addition, to further evaluate

the potential of 20G as a practical medium for space agriculture, follow-up trials were conducted 
using larger sample sizes and the paper towel pre-germination method across multiple bean 
species. Collectively, these results underscore the importance of integrating optimized pre-
germination protocols with adaptive moisture management strategies to improve plant 
establishment in extreme or resource-limited environments. 
3.4 Seedling Growth in 100R with Self-Watering System and Pre-Germination 
A self-watering system was implemented (Figure 12A) to maintain consistent hydration, 
and preliminary viability tests were conducted to assess its effectiveness. In the initial experiment, 
various soil mixtures—comprising regolith, garden soil, fertilizer, root growth enhancer, coconut 
oil, water-mixed gelatin, and gelatin powder—were tested for plant growth (Table 3). Prior to 
planting, seeds were pre-germinated using the paper towel method, with four seeds placed per 
Petri dish to maximize sprouting success for each variety. During planting, two seeds of the same 
type were placed into three different pots, each containing one of the three prepared soil mixtures. 
The self-watering system was intended to provide continuous moisture without manual 
intervention. However, due to insufficient oversight over a weekend, mold developed in the 
mixtures, killing all plants except one in the 100% regolith condition—which had been placed in a 
separate grow box unaffected by the mold outbreak. Despite this setback, the 100R pot in the 
self-watering setup successfully supported the growth of a single Great Northern Bean. The 
system maintained adequate moisture without the need for manual watering. Qualitative 
observations also revealed that the growth medium in the self-watering setup was looser and less 
compacted than that in the manually watered 100R pot, suggesting enhanced aeration and root 
development potential.

3.5 Confirming 20G as a Viable Growth Medium for Space Agriculture 
To confirm the potential of 20G as a practical medium for agriculture in space, a follow-up 
trial was conducted using a larger sample size and the paper towel pre-germination method 
across multiple bean species. As shown in Figure 14, larger garden pots were used and separated 
into 4 distinct sections containing the following seed distributions: Great Northern Beans (n = 4), 
Burpee’s Stringless Green Beans (n = 4), Tendergreen Improved Beans (n = 4), and Broad 
Windsor Fava Beans (n = 2). Each bean was pre-germinated using the paper towel method for 
24 hours before planting. Due to the larger size of the Broad Windsor Fava Beans after pre-
germination, only two beans were planted in its designated region compared to the four beans in 
other regions.

Under the 20G medium and 24-hour pre-germination conditions, all four bean species

the 24-hour water soaking approach (Tables 1-2, Figures 5-7), despite the expectation that 
extending pre-germination to the radicle or root hair stage would likely result in further 
improvements in both germination efficiency and early seedling growth.

needed to assess longer-term growth dynamics, the growth period limited data collection to 14

4. Discussion 
This study explored the varied combinations of germination method, growth media 
composition, and seed developmental stage at time of planting which revealed critical factors that 
influence plant development in simulated lunar environments. The findings strongly support the

32 
 
 
hypothesis that both the composition of the growth medium and the physiological readiness of 
the seeds play decisive roles in successful early plant development. 
4.1 The Impact of Germination Method 
Seeds germinated through the paper towel method consistently outperformed those 
germinated through the water soaking method (Figure 1). The success of the paper towel method 
is likely attributable to its ability to maintain optimal moisture conditions while preventing 
oversaturation. This controlled environment supports aerobic respiration and encourages uniform 
root development, both of which are critical for successful early seedling establishment. In 
contrast, seeds soaked in water often experienced delayed or failed germination, likely due to low 
oxygen diffusion and excessive water retention. While water soaking may serve as a useful pre-
treatment for some bean species with moderately firm seed coats—such as Broad Windsor Fava 
Beans, which germinated across all tested growth media following water soaking (Tables 1-2; 
Figures 1 and 7)—it is not effective as a standalone germination method for promoting optimal 
and consistent seedling development. 
4.2 Developmental Stage at Transplanting Influences Growth 
The results from this study demonstrate that advancing seeds to later developmental 
stages, such as radicle emergence or root hair development, significantly enhances seedling 
growth, particularly under challenging conditions like regolith simulants. Pre-germinating seeds 
allowed for faster emergence, earlier leaf development, and improved overall seedling growth 
compared to the 24-hour soaking method (Table 1; Figures 6, 9, and 17; Figure 11). For both 
Burpee’s Stringless Green Pod Beans and Great Northern Beans, pre-germination resulted in 
faster growth and more robust plants across various media. Specifically, seedlings from the 
radicle emergence stage showed improved growth rate, height, leaf area, and leaf emergence, 
with development accelerated compared to the soaking group. The root behavior observed in 
100R suggests adaptive growth responses to limited aeration and moisture, further highlighting

33 
 
 
the importance of seed developmental stage in optimizing growth under resource-constrained 
conditions. 
4.3 Effects of Media Composition on Plant Development 
The media tested in this study revealed distinct differences in their ability to support early 
seedling development, highlighting the critical roles of nutrient availability, aeration, and structural 
properties. While the organic-rich 100S medium consistently supported optimal growth, regolith-
dominant substrates limited performance due to their inherent physical and chemical constraints. 
Among the mixed compositions, the 20G blend, incorporating both soil and gelatin, demonstrated 
strong potential by sustaining growth across multiple species under suboptimal conditions 
(Figures 15–19). Species-specific responses further underscored varying degrees of tolerance to 
regolith-based media. In particular, Broad Windsor Fava Bean exhibited notable resilience and 
consistent development even in pure regolith, reinforcing its potential for space-based cultivation.. 
These outcomes suggest that hybrid media like 20G may offer a viable solution for balancing 
biological needs with resource limitations in extraterrestrial agriculture. 
4.4 Benefits of a Self-Watering System 
The integration of a self-watering system ensured consistent hydration and demonstrated 
the efficacy of the self-watering system in sustaining early seedling establishment in pure regolith 
following root hair-stage pre-germination. The rapid emergence and steady growth observed in 
all of the six bean varieties (Figure 12 and Figure 13; Table 4) underscore the advantages of 
combining physiological readiness with consistent moisture availability. Overall, this approach 
effectively addressed the low water retention, supporting early growth without manual watering. 
Additionally, the looser soil observed through the self-watering method addressed the structural 
limitations of regolith by improving aeration, alleviating the potential hypoxic conditions of the 
manually watered regolith. These findings underscore the value of integrating pre-germination 
protocols with passive watering systems to enhance plant establishment in resource-limited or 
extraterrestrial agricultural environments. Additionally, this approach offers a scalable solution for

34 
 
 
reducing water usage while addressing regolith's low porosity and poor water retention, two 
significant challenges in extraterrestrial agriculture. 
4.5 Limitations of the Current Study 
Some limitations of this study include the limited time frame for our main experiment due 
to the need to replant after most of our plants died in the initial/preliminary experiment. The mold 
growth that killed every plant except for the 100R plant in the separate grow box likely formed due 
to insufficient care over the weekend and excessive soil moisture. The limited time frame of the 
growth period restricted the maximum observation period to 27 days. If we had more time for 
observation and data collection, more significant differences, such as additional leaves and 
flowering, could have been observed—especially for the Broad Windsor Fava Beans, which 
exhibited significant growth after the growth period. Furthermore, due to the limited regolith after 
our initial/preliminary experiment, this study planted many bean species in one pot, which may 
have limited growth due to cramped growing space and competition between beans. Another 
limitation was the necessity of 50% regolith in the soil mixture. If there was more flexibility in the 
amount of regolith in the mixture, the experiment could have yielded a wider range of success 
from different ratios of gelatin, soil, and regolith. 
4.6 Conclusion and Future Directions 
Overall, our results demonstrate that early plant growth in regolith-based media can be 
improved through a combination of pre-germination techniques, ideal media composition, and 
watering methods. While pure regolith remains a challenging medium, the Broad Windsor Fava 
Bean demonstrated notable adaptability. The 20G mixture performed slightly better than 50SR in 
promoting germination and growth, suggesting that moderate gelatin supplementation can 
improve water retention without significantly compromising aeration. Since the differences 
between growth in the 50SR and 20G mixtures were not exceptionally large, it can be concluded 
that a more effective use of gelatin could be an additional treatment rather than a 20% inclusion, 
so that it could be used as a supplement for the plants rather than a replacement of soil. In contrast,

35 
 
 
high-gelatin content mixtures (50G and 50SG) inhibited growth, likely due to excess moisture and 
limited gas exchange. These results highlight the importance of optimizing additive concentrations 
and media structure to balance hydration with oxygen availability. Furthermore, despite the similar 
growth in plant height, there was still a noticeable difference in leaf size compared to the 100S 
control which compromises the plant’s ability to photosynthesize. This indicates that further 
research is needed to explore nutrient additives to address the deficiencies in our current media 
compositions. 
Future research should explore a broader range of gelatin concentrations across diverse 
regolith-soil mixtures to determine the optimal balance between water retention, aeration, and 
microbial stability.In addition, studies should assess the influence of extraterrestrial environmental 
conditions—particularly reduced lunar gravity—on plant morphology, physiology, and growth 
rates. Long-term cultivation trials will also be essential to evaluate sustained growth, yield, and 
overall plant resilience, thereby advancing the viability of regenerative agricultural systems for 
future lunar and off-Earth missions.
